what_its_for: Lithium carbonate is used to treat bipolar disorder (also called manic-depressive illness). It helps control episodes of mania (extreme highs) and can help prevent future mood swings. Your doctor may also use it for other conditions not listed here.
how_to_take: Take lithium exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablets or capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or break them, especially the extended-release (ER) form. Take it with food or milk to help prevent an upset stomach. Try to take it at the same times every day to keep a steady level of the medicine in your body. Drink 8 to 10 glasses of water or fluids every day unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
dosing: Your doctor will set your dose based on blood tests that measure the level of lithium in your body. A common starting dose for adults is 300 mg taken 2 to 3 times daily. Your dose may be slowly increased until the right level is reached. For extended-release tablets, dosing is often twice daily. Never change your dose on your own. Your blood levels will need to be checked regularly, especially when you first start or if your dose changes.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and remember within 2 hours of when you were supposed to take it, go ahead and take it. If it has been more than 2 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one, as this can cause dangerous side effects.
storage: Store lithium at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the container tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused medicine properly — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid major changes in the amount of salt (sodium) you eat, since low salt intake can cause lithium levels in your blood to rise to dangerous levels. Do not go on a low-salt diet without talking to your doctor. Avoid becoming dehydrated — activities that cause heavy sweating (like intense exercise or being in very hot weather), vomiting, or diarrhea can raise lithium levels to dangerous amounts. Drink plenty of fluids. Limit or avoid alcohol, as it can make side effects worse. Avoid caffeine in large amounts, as it can affect your lithium level. Use caution with over-the-counter medicines — NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) and certain blood pressure medicines can raise lithium levels dangerously. Always check with your pharmacist or doctor before taking any new medicine, including vitamins and supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice signs of lithium toxicity (too much lithium in your body), including: shaking or tremors that get worse, muscle twitching or weakness, slurred speech, confusion or feeling very drowsy, dizziness or loss of coordination, blurry vision, irregular or fast heartbeat, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is severe or does not stop, or seizures. Also contact your doctor if you have signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Let your doctor know if you develop frequent urination, increased thirst, or unusual weight gain, as these can be signs your kidneys or thyroid are being affected.
when_it_works: It may take 1 to 3 weeks before you notice improvement in your symptoms, and sometimes it can take several weeks to feel the full benefit. Do not stop taking lithium even if you feel better — stopping suddenly can cause your symptoms to return. Lithium is often taken long-term to help prevent future mood episodes.
special_populations: Older adults: Use with extra caution. Older patients are more sensitive to lithium and more likely to experience side effects. Lower doses are often needed and more frequent blood level checks may be required. Pregnancy: Lithium can harm an unborn baby, especially during the first trimester (first 3 months). Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits with you. Breastfeeding: Lithium passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Safety and dosing in children under 12 have not been well established. Use only under close medical supervision. Kidney or heart problems: Lithium is removed from the body by the kidneys, so people with kidney disease or heart problems may need lower doses and closer monitoring. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions before starting lithium.
